questions.q: On a hot May afternoon Neha sees white patches near the armpits of her school shirt. Next morning she sees small droplets on the leaves of the rose bush and the lawn grass. Which characteristic of living beings links the two observations?
questions.a: Excretion, the removal of waste products from the body
o: Excretion, the removal of waste products from the body
Respiration, the movement of air in and out of the body
Response to a stimulus, here the heat of the summer sun
Nutrition, the taking in of water and salts for growth

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The touch-me-not plant is a living being.
Reason (R): The touch-me-not plant does not move from one place to another.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: In the school garden, Rohan sees a small green caterpillar lying still on a guava leaf for twenty minutes. His sister says it may still be alive. Which way of deciding fits the chapter best?
questions.a: Watch it over time for signs such as response to touch, growth or excretion
o: Watch it over time for signs such as response to touch, growth or excretion
Decide at once: anything that is not moving right now must be non-living
Call it living only if it moves on its own, since moving on its own means living
Call it living because it sits on a living leaf, so it must be alive too

questions.q:
Riya writes in her notebook: 'When I stepped on a thorn, pulling my foot back was the stimulus and the thorn was my response.'
(a) Correct her sentence, saying what makes something a stimulus.
(b) Write a plant example from the chapter in the same form, naming the stimulus first and the response second.
questions.a: (a) She has swapped them. Stepping on the thorn is the stimulus, because a stimulus is any thing or event that prompts a living being to respond; pulling the foot back is the response. (b) A touch on a touch-me-not (chhui-mui) plant is the stimulus; the folding of its leaves is the response.
s: Part (a): thorn as the stimulus, pulling back as the response, with the meaning of stimulus
Part (b): plant example with stimulus (touch) and response (leaves fold) in the right order

questions.q: Ravi counts 72 breaths in 4 minutes after a slow walk and 108 breaths in 3 minutes after a run. After the run he takes ___ more breaths per minute than after the walk.
A small fly walks into the saucer-shaped leaf of a Drosera plant. The hair-like projections with sticky ends bend inward and hold it. What does this observation show?
questions.a: A plant can move a part of its body without changing its place
o: A plant can move a part of its body without changing its place
A plant can change its place when it needs food from insects
The leaf is excreting a sticky waste that happens to trap insects
The leaf is only growing larger, which is not a form of movement

questions.q: Kiran finds a closed snail shell on her garden wall. It does not move for an hour. Plan how she could find out over one week whether it holds a living snail. Name five characteristics of living beings she could look for, and say what she would expect to see for each if the snail is alive.
questions.a: Any five, each with an observation: (1) movement: the shell is in a new place on the wall next morning; (2) need for food: leaves near it are nibbled; (3) growth: over a long time the shell becomes larger; (4) response to a stimulus: a gentle touch makes the soft body pull into the shell; (5) excretion: waste is left on the wall where it rested; (6) reproduction: young snails appear near it. If none of these appear even with food, air and water around, it would be dead or empty.
s: Movement with an expected observation
Need for food with an expected observation
Response to a stimulus with an expected observation
Excretion or growth with an expected observation
Reproduction or another characteristic with an expected observation

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Leaves of the amla tree that face each other come together after sunset, which is a response to a stimulus.
Statement 2: A car moves on the road and uses fuel, so by the chapter's list of characteristics it must be counted as living.
Statement 3: A potted plant that dries up only because nobody watered it fits the chapter's description of death exactly.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Aarav says: 'Anything that moves on its own is living, and anything that does not move from place to place is non-living.' Check his claim using one example for each half.
questions.a: No, both halves are wrong. A car moves on the road but does not grow, respire or reproduce, so it is non-living. A plant does not move from place to place but grows, respires and reproduces, and even shows movements such as flowers opening, so it is living. Movement alone does not decide.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
First half disproved with an example such as a car
Second half disproved with an example such as a plant

questions.q: A toy robot dog in a shop walks across the floor, wags its tail and has to be charged every night. Which reason correctly places it among non-living things?
questions.a: It moves, but it cannot grow or produce young ones of its own kind
o: It moves, but it cannot grow or produce young ones of its own kind
It moves, and living beings such as plants never show any movement
It needs charging, and living beings never need anything from outside
It has no stomata, and every living being takes in air through stomata

questions.q:
A packet of bean seeds has lain in a kitchen jar for a year without any change.
(a) Name one characteristic of living beings that the seeds do not seem to show in the jar.
(b) Why is that alone not enough to call the seeds non-living? Use what happens when they are given the right conditions.
questions.a: (a) Growth (or movement or response; any one). (b) Given water and air, as in moist soil, the seeds germinate into sprouts and grow, so they can show the characteristics of life once the conditions are available.
s: Part (a): one characteristic the stored seed does not show, such as growth
Part (b): with water and air the seed germinates and grows, so lack of change in the jar does not prove it non-living

questions.q:
Match each observation with the characteristic of living beings it shows, as the chapter groups them.
Column I
1. The abdomen of a resting buffalo rises and falls
2. Droplets of water appear on rose leaves at dawn
3. Leaves of an amla branch come together after sunset
4. A climber winds itself around a bamboo pole
Column II
a. Movement
b. Excretion
c. Respiration
d. Response to a stimulus

Two Class 6 students at a school in Nagpur counted their breaths per minute after three activities.
Riya: 18 after a normal walk, 36 after a run, 27 after a few dance steps.
Arjun: 20 after a normal walk, 34 after a run, 30 after a few dance steps.
(a) Breathing is part of which process? Say which way the air moves when Riya breathes in and when she breathes out.
(b) Riya says, 'I respired only after the run; on the walk I was just walking.' Use the counts to correct her, and say whose breaths per minute rose more from the walk to the run, and by how many.
(c) The teacher says this process goes on in the school's neem tree too, though it has no nose. Through what does a plant take air in and out, and where are they found?
(d) The class can do one follow-up: watch a resting cow's abdomen, or ask senior students to show leaf pores under a microscope. Using your answers to (b) and (c), which better supports 'all living beings respire'? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Respiration; when she breathes in, air moves from outside to inside her body, and when she breathes out, from inside to outside. (b) She breathed 18 times a minute even after the walk, and breathing is part of respiration, which goes on all the time in all living beings; the run only made her breathe faster. Riya rose by 36 - 18 = 18 per minute and Arjun by 34 - 20 = 14, so Riya's rose more, by 4 breaths per minute. (c) Tiny pores called stomata, on the surface of leaves. (d) The microscope: the counts in (b) already show breathing in humans, and a cow is one more animal, while the stomata of (c) show the same process in a plant, where it cannot be seen with the eye. (The cow is accepted if justified as easy to watch without equipment, with the note that it adds no plant.)
s: Part (a): respiration, with the direction of air on breathing in and out
Part (b): respiration goes on during the walk too (18 a minute); Riya's rise larger, by 4 (18 against 14)
Part (c): stomata on the surface of leaves
Part (d): a choice that weighs adding a plant against ease of observation

questions.q: Ishita is collecting evidence that the touch-me-not (chhui-mui) in her school garden is a living being. Which of her notes does NOT show a characteristic of living beings?
questions.a: It stays fixed in one spot in the garden all year round
o: It stays fixed in one spot in the garden all year round
Its leaves fold up within seconds when her friend touches them
New touch-me-not plants come up from it near the old plant
Tiny pores on its leaves let air move in and out of the plant

questions.q: True or False? A field of sunflowers never moves from its place, so the sunflowers fail the movement test for living beings. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Plants do not move from one place to another, but they show movements such as the opening of flowers, the inward bending of Drosera hairs and climbers winding round a support, so a fixed place does not mean no movement.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: plants show movement without changing place, with an example such as flowers opening

questions.q: Two potted tulsi plants are left in a hostel over the vacation. Plant P gets no water at all and dries up. Plant Q gets water, air and sunlight every day, yet it yellows, stops growing and all its life activities end. Which plant matches the chapter's description of death exactly, and why does the other not match it word for word?
questions.a: Plant Q. The chapter calls a living being dead when it cannot show the characteristics of life even though the resources it needs (food, air, water) are available; Q had them. Plant P lost its life activities because water was not available, so it does not fit the 'despite the resources' wording.
s: Plant Q identified
Reason: life activities ended even though water, air and food were available
Plant P explained: water was withheld, so the 'despite resources' condition is not met

questions.q:
Meena says her cricket bat is living because it is made of willow wood, and wood comes from a tree.
(a) Is Meena right? Give one characteristic of living beings that the bat does not show.
(b) Why does 'made from a living thing' not decide whether something is living now?
questions.a: (a) No; the bat does not grow (also: does not respire, excrete, respond to stimuli or reproduce). (b) Whether a thing is living depends on whether it shows the characteristics of life itself; the bat shows none of them, whatever it was made from.
s: Part (a): not living, with one missing characteristic such as growth
Part (b): the test is whether the thing itself shows life's characteristics, not its origin

questions.q: A student wants to classify four things: a car, a burning candle (it needs air and gets shorter), a balloon (it gets bigger when blown into) and a chick. For each thing, name the feature that might mislead someone and the characteristic of life that decides the answer. Then state the rule you used.
questions.a: (1) Car: it moves, but it does not grow, respire or reproduce, so non-living. (2) Candle: it needs air, but it does not grow, excrete or reproduce, so non-living. (3) Balloon: it gets bigger, but only when air is blown in; it does not grow by itself using food and does not reproduce, so non-living. (4) Chick: it moves, eats, grows, breathes, excretes, responds and will reproduce, so living. Rule: a living being shows all the characteristics of life; absence of any of them shows a non-living thing.
s: Car: misleading movement, decided by no growth or reproduction
Candle: misleading need for air, decided by no growth or reproduction
Balloon: misleading increase in size, decided by no growth through food or reproduction
Chick: shows all the characteristics, so living
Rule: absence of any characteristic indicates a non-living thing

questions.q:
Tanu's frock from four years ago no longer fits her, but the frock bought at the same time for her doll still fits the doll.
(a) Which characteristic of living beings does this comparison show in Tanu, and why does the doll not show it?
(b) Tanu's brother says she grew 'just because the years passed'. Which other characteristic from the chapter must go with growth, and how does the chapter link the two?
questions.a: (a) Growth: Tanu has become larger in size, while the doll is non-living and does not grow. (b) The need for food (nutrition): the chapter says living beings need food for their growth and development, so time alone does not make her grow.
s: Part (a): growth shown by Tanu, not by the non-living doll
Part (b): need for food, since living beings need food for growth and development

questions.q:
In one school week the eco-club recorded these observations.
Touch-me-not: touched 12 times; its leaves folded within seconds every time.
Amla tree: leaves facing each other came together each evening after sunset.
Rose bush: small droplets on the leaves on 5 of the 7 mornings.
Bitter-gourd climber: wound once more round its bamboo stick.
Drosera in the science lab: its hairs had bent inward over two small insects that entered its leaves.
(a) Which characteristic of living beings do the rose droplets show, and what is the plant removing in them?
(b) A classmate writes, 'The climber stays in its pot, so it shows no movement.' Correct him using the chapter.
(c) Which two plants in the table does the chapter use as its examples of response to a stimulus, and for which of the two can you name the stimulus from the table?
(d) Juniors will visit at 11 a.m. on a 'plants respond to stimuli' tour, with time for one plant: the touch-me-not or the Drosera. Which should they see, and what does the other plant offer that the chosen one does not?
questions.a: (a) Excretion; the plant removes excess water and minerals as small droplets. (b) Plants do not move from one place to another, but they do show movements; climbers wind themselves around an object placed close to them, as this one did round its stick. (c) The touch-me-not and the amla; the stimulus can be named only for the touch-me-not (touch). (d) The touch-me-not is the stronger choice: the juniors can give the stimulus themselves and see the leaves fold within seconds, as all 12 touches showed. The Drosera's hairs move only when an insect enters, which may not happen during a short visit, though the trapped insects show a plant moving a part of its body to catch its food. Choosing the Drosera is accepted if the answer weighs this.
s: Part (a): excretion of excess water and minerals
Part (b): plants show movement without changing place, such as climbers winding round a support
Part (c): touch-me-not and amla, with touch named for the touch-me-not
Part (d): a choice weighing a response seen at once against an insect that may not come

questions.q: Write a short situation (two or three lines) set in your home, garden or school in which a plant from the chapter responds to a stimulus that you can name. Then name the stimulus and the response.
questions.a: E.g. During recess Kabir brushes past a chhui-mui plant by the school gate and its leaves fold up at once. Stimulus: the touch of his hand. Response: the folding of the leaves. (The amla's leaves coming together after sunset are a response too, but the chapter does not name their stimulus, so they do not suit this task.)
s: A believable situation with a plant from the chapter
Stimulus named correctly
Response named correctly

questions.q: A farmer near Vijayawada sowed groundnut seeds. Next day a flood left water standing above the soil for two weeks, under bright sun. Almost no seeds sprouted. Which explanation fits the chapter's idea that seeds use the air in the spaces between soil particles?
questions.a: Water filled the gaps between soil particles, so seeds got no air
o: Water filled the gaps between soil particles, so seeds got no air
The bright sunlight on the field stopped the seeds from germinating
So much water hardened the seed coat instead of softening it
The seeds needed darkness, and the flooded field was too bright

questions.q:
Four trays of mung seeds are set up for a week.
Tray P: dry cotton, on a sunny window sill.
Tray Q: seeds completely under water, on the window sill.
Tray R: moist cotton, inside a closed cupboard.
Tray S: moist cotton, on the window sill.
In which trays should the seeds germinate?
questions.a: Trays R and S only
o: Trays R and S only
Tray S only
Trays Q and S only
Trays Q, R and S only

questions.q: Lina's bean seeds sprouted well in moist soil inside a dark cupboard. A week later the seedlings were pale, thin and weak. To keep them growing she must now give them ___.
questions.a: sunlight

questions.q:
Two pots of bean seeds stood on a sunny terrace for 15 days, and neither sprouted. Pot 1 was never watered. For Pot 2 the watering record is lost.
(a) Name two different conditions, either of which could explain Pot 2's failure.
(b) What could you look for in Pot 2's soil to tell which of the two it was?
questions.a: (a) Too little water (the seed coat was never softened), or too much water (water standing above the soil fills the spaces between soil particles, so the seeds get no air). Light is not the cause: the pot was in sunlight, and light is not essential for germination anyway. (b) Dry, hard soil points to missing water; soggy soil with water standing on top points to missing air.
s: Part (a): no water and excess water (no air) as the two possible causes
Part (b): dry soil for missing water, standing water for missing air

questions.q: The school kitchen garden must raise 40 healthy bean seedlings for Van Mahotsav week. Write a five-step plan that takes the seeds from the packet to seedlings ready to plant out, and give the chapter's reason for each step.
questions.a: Any five steps with reasons: (1) Soak the seeds overnight: water softens the seed coat and helps the embryo develop. (2) Sow them in loose garden soil, not packed soil: seeds use the air in the spaces between soil particles, and the spaces let roots grow easily. (3) Water moderately every day to keep the soil slightly moist: seeds need water to germinate. (4) Never let water stand above the soil: it would fill the soil spaces and the seeds would get no air. (5) The seeds may sprout in the shade or in a store-room, since most seeds do not need light to germinate, but the seedlings must then be kept in sunlight, which they need for further growth.
s: Soaking, with the seed-coat reason
Loose soil, with the air and root reason
Moderate daily watering, with the water reason
No standing water, with the air reason
Sunlight after sprouting, with light not needed for germination itself

questions.q: Before sowing, Rahul's grandmother soaks chana seeds in water overnight. Which idea from the chapter supports this practice?
questions.a: Water softens the seed coat and helps the embryo inside develop
o: Water softens the seed coat and helps the embryo inside develop
Water removes the seed coat so the seed no longer needs any air
Water keeps out light, and seeds need darkness to germinate
Water replaces soil, so the soaked seed need not be sown at all

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bean seeds sown in loose garden soil grow longer roots than bean seeds sown in soil stamped down hard.
Reason (R): Seeds use the air in the spaces between soil particles for germination.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Riddhi compares only two pots: Pot 1 has dry soil in sunlight, and Pot 2 has moist soil in the dark. Pot 2 germinates and Pot 1 does not. She concludes that darkness helps germination. Show that her two pots cannot support that conclusion.
questions.a: Two conditions differ between the pots: water (dry versus moist) and light (sunlight versus dark). The result could be due to the water alone, so she cannot tell what darkness did. To test light she must change only light: moist soil in the dark against moist soil in sunlight.
s: Both water and light differ between the pots
The result can be explained by water, so the effect of light is unknown
A fair pair that changes only light is named

questions.q: Diya wants to test only whether light affects the germination of bean seeds. Which two pots should she compare?
questions.a: Moist soil in the dark and moist soil in sunlight
o: Moist soil in the dark and moist soil in sunlight
Dry soil in sunlight and moist soil in sunlight
Waterlogged soil in sunlight and moist soil in the dark
Dry soil in sunlight and waterlogged soil in sunlight

questions.q:
Neel puts one tray of moist bean seeds inside a cold box, which is dark inside, and another tray of moist bean seeds on a warm, sunny window sill. He says any difference in sprouting will be due to temperature alone.
(a) What else differs between his two trays?
(b) Using the chapter's finding about light, how much is this likely to spoil his germination result?
(c) How should he change the set-up so that it is a fair test of temperature?
questions.a: (a) Light: one tray is in the dark and the other in sunlight. (b) Most seeds, beans included, do not need light to germinate, so the light difference is unlikely to change the sprouting much; but two things still differ, so he cannot be sure the result is due to temperature alone. (c) Keep both trays in the dark (or both in the light), with the same seeds, number, moisture and air, and change only the temperature.
s: Part (a): light also differs
Part (b): light is not essential for germination, but the test is still not fair
Part (c): only temperature changed, everything else kept the same

questions.q:
For a plant sale, the Class 6 eco-club tested four trays of 20 bean seeds each for 10 days.
Tray 1: moist soil, sunny window: 17 sprouted.
Tray 2: moist soil, dark store-room: 18 sprouted.
Tray 3: dry soil, sunny window: 0 sprouted.
Tray 4: water standing above the soil, sunny window: 0 sprouted.
(a) Name the condition for germination that Tray 3 lacked and the one that Tray 4 lacked.
(b) Work out the percentage that sprouted in Trays 1 and 2. Sohan says the higher figure proves that darkness helps germination. Is the gap big enough to say so?
(c) The club needs healthy seedlings to sell four weeks later. Should it raise them in the store-room or at the window? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Tray 3 lacked water; Tray 4 lacked air, because the standing water filled the spaces between soil particles. (b) 17/20 = 85% and 18/20 = 90%. The gap is one seed out of 20, too small to prove anything; together with the chapter's finding that light is not essential for germination, the fair reading is that light made no real difference. (c) The window (or sprout them anywhere and then move them to the window): sprouting was about the same in both places, but after germination sunlight is needed for the seedlings' further growth, so plants kept in the store-room would not be fit to sell.
s: Part (a): water missing in Tray 3, air missing in Tray 4
Part (b): 85% and 90%, a one-seed gap that does not show darkness helps
Part (c): the window chosen, because seedlings need sunlight to grow after germination

questions.q:
A packet of bean seeds says: 'Water lightly every day. Do not let water stand on the soil.'
(a) Give the chapter's reason for 'water lightly every day'.
(b) Give the chapter's reason for 'do not let water stand on the soil'.
questions.a: (a) Seeds need water to germinate: water softens the seed coat and helps the tiny embryo inside develop into a plant. (b) Standing water fills the spaces between soil particles, and seeds use the air in those spaces, so they would get no air.
s: Part (a): water softens the seed coat so the embryo can develop
Part (b): standing water takes the place of air in the soil spaces

questions.q:
Read the statements about bean seeds in pots.
Statement 1: In a pot where water always stands above the soil, the seeds do not get air.
Statement 2: Most seeds need light to germinate, so a pot kept in the dark cannot show germination.
Statement 3: After germination, the seedling needs sunlight for its further growth.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: A farmer explains four of her sowing habits. Which explanation would the chapter NOT back?
questions.a: I sow only on bright days, because bean seeds cannot sprout without light
o: I sow only on bright days, because bean seeds cannot sprout without light
I soak the seeds overnight, because water softens the hard seed coat
I dig the soil loose first, so that the young roots can push through easily
I never let water stand on the field, so the seeds get air from the soil

questions.q:
Meena sows two batches of bean seeds in the same moist, loose soil. Batch 1 was soaked in water overnight; Batch 2 was put in dry from the packet. Batch 1 sprouts two days earlier.
(a) Which part of the seed did the soaking act on first, and how did that help?
(b) Why did Batch 2 still sprout, only later?
questions.a: (a) The seed coat: water softens it and helps the tiny embryo inside to develop, so the soaked seeds were ready sooner. (b) The moist soil gave Batch 2 water (and the soil spaces gave air), so its seed coats softened too, but they first had to take up the water in the soil.
s: Part (a): soaking softened the seed coat, letting the embryo develop
Part (b): the moist soil supplied water and air, so Batch 2 softened later

questions.q:
Ritu wrote this report on the four-pot germination activity. Say whether each sentence is correct or wrong, and correct the wrong ones.
1. 'Pot A, dry and in sunlight, did not germinate because it had no water.'
2. 'Pot B had water standing above the soil, so its seeds had the most air of all.'
3. 'Pot C, moist and in the dark, germinated, so bean seeds do not need light to germinate.'
4. 'Water helps germination by making the seed coat harder, which protects the embryo.'
5. 'The seedlings in Pot C will keep growing well even if they stay in the dark.'
questions.a: 1. Correct: water was the missing condition. 2. Wrong: standing water fills the spaces between soil particles, so the seeds in Pot B got no air. 3. Correct. 4. Wrong: water softens the seed coat and helps the tiny embryo inside develop into a plant. 5. Wrong: after germination, sunlight is needed for the further growth of the seedling.
s: Sentence 1 judged correct
Sentence 2 corrected: standing water means no air
Sentence 3 judged correct
Sentence 4 corrected: water softens the seed coat
Sentence 5 corrected: seedlings need sunlight to keep growing

questions.q: True or False? Meena peels the softened seed coat off a soaked bean seed and says, 'I have thrown away the part that would have grown into the new plant.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The seed coat is only the outer covering of the seed; the part that develops into a plant is the tiny embryo inside it. Soaking helps because water softens the seed coat and so helps the embryo to develop.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the seed coat is the outer covering; the embryo inside develops into the plant

questions.q: Priya fills a pot with soil from a building site, packed hard like a brick. She sows bean seeds, waters them moderately and keeps the pot in sunlight. Only a few seeds sprout, and their roots stay short and bent. Which explanation fits the chapter?
o: Packed soil has few spaces, so less air for seeds and less room for roots
Packed soil blocks out the sunlight that seeds need in order to germinate
Packed soil makes the seed coat too wet, so the embryo inside cannot develop
Packed soil hardens the seed coat, so the embryo grows into a short root
questions.a: Packed soil has few spaces, so less air for seeds and less room for roots

questions.q: Sameer says: 'Seeds need water and air to germinate, and they need sunlight too; that is why the seeds in the dark pot failed.' Check his claim against the pot activity in the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Seeds do need the right amount of water and air. But light is not essential for germinating bean seeds: in the activity the moist pot kept in the dark did germinate, so a dark pot does not fail for want of light.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: water and air are needed
Wrong part: the moist pot in the dark germinated, so light is not essential

questions.q: A shopkeeper stores rajma in a dark storeroom and says, 'Darkness will stop them sprouting.' Evaluate his plan using the chapter, and suggest what actually prevents sprouting.
questions.a: The plan is weak: most seeds, including beans, do not need light to germinate, so darkness alone will not stop sprouting. Keeping the rajma dry prevents it, because without water the seed coat does not soften and the embryo cannot develop.
s: Darkness rejected: light is not needed for germination
Keeping the grains dry, because seeds need water to germinate

questions.q:
Class 6 in Guntur sowed 30 bean seeds in each of three garden beds, all in sunlight.
Bed L: loose garden soil, watered moderately every day: 27 sprouted, with long roots.
Bed P: soil stamped down hard after sowing, watered the same way: 15 sprouted, with short, bent roots.
Bed W: loose soil in a corner the hose reached on only 3 of the 10 days: 12 sprouted.
(a) Which condition for germination did Bed W often lack, and what does that condition do for a seed?
(b) Give two chapter reasons why Bed P did worse than Bed L, one for the fewer sprouts and one for the short roots.
(c) How many more seeds sprouted in Bed L than in Bed P, as a percentage of the 30 sown?
(d) Before the next sowing the school can fix only one bed: lay a longer hose pipe to Bed W, or dig and loosen Bed P by hand. If the fixed bed then does as well as Bed L, which fix gains more seedlings, and what else should the school weigh?
questions.a: (a) Water; it softens the seed coat and helps the embryo inside develop into a plant. (b) Fewer sprouts: packed soil has few spaces between particles, and seeds use the air in those spaces. Short roots: the spaces between soil particles allow roots to grow easily. (c) 27 - 15 = 12 seeds, which is 12/30 = 40% of the seeds sown. (d) Fixing Bed W gains 27 - 12 = 15 seedlings; fixing Bed P gains 27 - 15 = 12. The hose gains more, but it costs money; loosening Bed P costs only effort and also gives the roots room to grow for the rest of the season. Either choice is accepted if it uses both numbers and one such factor.
s: Part (a): water, which softens the seed coat for the embryo
Part (b): less air in packed soil, and no spaces for roots to grow easily
Part (c): 12 seeds, 40%
Part (d): gains of 15 and 12 compared and weighed against another factor

questions.q:

questions.q:
For a science-fair stall called 'Plants grow and move', a team tied a bean seedling upright on wet blotting paper in sunlight and measured its shoot every two days: Day 0: 2.0 cm, Day 2: 3.3 cm, Day 4: 5.1 cm, Day 6: 6.8 cm. On Day 6 they turned the plate upside down, so that the shoot pointed down and the root pointed up.
(a) What will the shoot and the root do over the next few days?
(b) Was the growth steady? Name the two-day spell with the most growth, give the average growth per day over the 6 days, and name the machine Jagadish Chandra Bose built that could measure how fast a plant grows.
(c) The stall has room for one more exhibit to show that 'plants sense light'. Choose between a seedling in a box lit through one hole, and a pair of seedlings watched for a week, one on a sunny sill and one in a dark cupboard. Justify your choice and say what the other exhibit would show.
questions.a: (a) The root bends and grows downward, and the shoot bends and grows upward. (b) Not steady: it grew 1.3 cm, 1.8 cm and 1.7 cm in the three spells, most between Day 2 and Day 4; 6.8 - 2.0 = 4.8 cm in 6 days is 0.8 cm per day on average. Bose's crescograph could measure how fast plants grow. (c) The box is the stronger choice: within a week its shoot visibly bends in the direction of the light from the hole, so visitors see the plant sensing where light comes from and responding. The sunny/dark pair shows that after germination a seedling needs sunlight for further growth, as the dark one grows weak, but that is a need for light more than a visible movement towards it, and the difference takes longer to show. The pair is accepted if the answer argues this.
s: Part (a): root bends down, shoot bends up
Part (b): not steady, most growth Day 2-4, 0.8 cm per day, crescograph
Part (c): a choice justified, with what the other exhibit would show (sunlight needed for growth vs bending towards light)

questions.q:
A class made this table from its own records and the chapter's frog life cycle.
Bean plant: seed sown Day 0; sprout (germination) Day 6; first leaves Day 11; first flowers Day 45; pods with seeds Day 62; plant yellow and dry by Day 85.
Frog: spawn Day 1; embryo Day 3-4; tadpole with tail Day 7-10; tadpole with hind legs 8-10 weeks; froglet 12 weeks; adult 14 weeks.
(a) In each row, at which stage is the next generation first carried, and in what form?
(b) Which row shows a change of habitat, and at which stage does it begin?
(c) Rahul says, 'The bean only gets bigger, while the frog really changes its body.' Judge his claim using both rows.
(d) What do the two rows share at their very end, and why does each cycle still continue?
(e) A project runs for a 10-week term (70 days) from Day 0. In which row can the class follow the cycle up to the stage that carries the next generation? Use the table.
questions.a: (a) Bean: the appearance of fruits, as the seeds inside the pods (Day 62). Frog: the adult stage, which reproduces and lays eggs as spawn. (b) The frog: eggs and tadpoles live in water; froglets (about 12 weeks) begin to spend some time on land, and adults live both in water and on land. (c) Partly right: the frog's body shape changes greatly (a tail appears and is lost, legs grow and become strong), but the bean does not only get bigger; it forms new structures, leaves, then flowers, then pods with seeds. (d) Both end in death (the bean plant dries even when watered); each cycle continues because, before that, reproduction gives new ones of the same kind: seeds for the bean, eggs for the frog. (e) The bean: its pods with seeds appear on Day 62, inside 70 days. The frog becomes an adult only at about 14 weeks (98 days); by Day 70 it is at most a tadpole with hind legs.
s: Part (a): bean, seeds in the pod; frog, the adult that lays eggs
Part (b): frog, from the froglet stage on land as well as water
Part (c): partly right, bean adds leaves, flowers and pods; frog changes body shape
Part (d): both end in death; reproduction (seeds, eggs) continues each cycle
Part (e): bean (Day 62 within 70); frog adult only at 98 days

questions.q:

s: Part (a): only germination, seed to sprout
Part (b): leaves, flowers, pods with seeds, i.e. on to the next generation of seeds

questions.q:
Ananya sowed 16 bean seeds in her kitchen garden in Pune, and 12 of them germinated. Later 8 plants flowered, and each of these produced 6 pods with 5 seeds in every pod.
(a) At which stage of the life cycle did the plants first carry the next generation, and in what form?
(b) How many seeds did the flowering plants produce in all, and why could the 4 germinated plants that never flowered give no seeds?
(c) Next season she wants about 60 plants. If her seeds germinate at this year's rate, how many seeds must she keep for sowing?
(d) In a wetter season two years ago, only 10 of 15 seeds germinated. Should she keep the number from (c), or 90 seeds? Use the numbers to justify.
questions.a: (a) The appearance of fruits: the seeds inside the pods. (b) 8 x 6 x 5 = 240 seeds. The 4 plants (12 - 8) that never flowered gave none, because the fruits with seeds develop from the flowers. (c) This year's rate is 12/16 = 75%, so 60 / 0.75 = 80 seeds. (d) At the wet-season rate of 10/15 (two out of three), 80 seeds give only about 53 plants, while 90 seeds give 60. Keeping 90 costs just 10 more of the 240 seeds (150 left to eat or share instead of 160), so it is a cheap safeguard if the season may be wet; 80 is enough if this year's rate holds. Either answer is accepted if it uses these numbers.
s: Part (a): fruit stage, as seeds in the pods
Part (b): 240 seeds; no flowers means no fruits, so no seeds
Part (c): 80 seeds at a 75% rate
Part (d): 80 against 90 judged with the two germination rates

questions.q:
Two bean seeds from the same pod are sown in moist, loose soil in two pots. Both sprout on Day 5. Pot X is then kept on a sunny window sill; Pot Y stays in a dark store-room, watered just like X.

(d) What does this mean for the next generation from each plant?
(e) Which characteristic of living beings, needed for the continuity of life, may Plant Y fail to show?
questions.a: (a) Germination needs the right amount of water and air, which both pots had; light is not essential for bean seeds to germinate. (b) Plant Y will not keep growing well and will stay weak, because after germination sunlight is needed for the further growth of the seedling. (c) The appearance of flowers and then of fruits, pods with seeds. (d) Plant X's seeds can be sown to start a new generation of bean plants; Plant Y is unlikely to give any seeds, so its part in the cycle stops. (e) Reproduction, producing new ones of its own kind (it may not reach it; growth is accepted for part credit, since Y also grows poorly).
s: Part (a): water and air present, light not essential for germination
Part (b): Y grows poorly, since seedlings need sunlight after germination
Part (c): flowers and fruits with seeds
Part (d): X's seeds continue the cycle, Y's line stops
Part (e): reproduction (growth earns partial credit)

questions.q: Newspapers and school notice boards ask people not to let water stagnate anywhere. Give two reasons, linked to the mosquito's life cycle, for this advice.
questions.a: The female mosquito lays eggs directly on or near water, so stagnant water gives her a place to lay them. The larvae and pupae live in water, so without stagnant water they cannot develop into adults.
s: Eggs are laid on or near water
Larvae and pupae need water to live and develop

questions.q:
Read the statements about mosquitoes.
Statement 1: An adult mosquito may survive for about 10 to 15 days.
Statement 2: The adult female mosquito lays her eggs directly on or near water.
Statement 3: The pupa looks almost the same as the adult mosquito, only smaller.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q:
A colony in Nagpur tried two plans for four weeks of the rainy season.
Block A: every Sunday, residents emptied and dried all coolers and pot trays.
Block B: residents did nothing for three weeks, then emptied everything once in week 4.
Larvae counted at sample sites each week: Block A 40, 12, 3, 2; Block B 38, 45, 52, 6.
Adults caught in traps in week 4: Block A 5; Block B 30.
(a) By what percentage did Block A's larvae count fall from week 1 to week 4?
(b) Explain that fall using the life cycle.
(c) Why did Block B's larvae count drop sharply in week 4?
(d) Why were many adults still caught in Block B in week 4, though its larvae count had dropped?
(e) Block A's plan is clearly the better one, yet its sites still had 2 larvae in week 4. Suggest one improvement to it and name the stage of the life cycle your improvement acts on.
questions.a: (a) (40 - 2) / 40 = 38/40 = 95%. (b) Each weekly emptying removed the water in which larvae and pupae live, so few could grow on to adults, and with fewer adults fewer eggs were laid on or near water. (c) Emptying removed the water the larvae were living in, so they could not survive. (d) In weeks 1 to 3 many larvae had already become pupae and then adults; adults fly away from the water and may survive 10 to 15 days, so emptying in week 4 did not touch them. (e) Any one improvement with its stage, e.g. cover water tanks and drums that cannot be emptied, so the female cannot lay eggs on that water (egg stage); empty twice a week, so larvae are removed before they become pupae and adults (larva and pupa); turn unused containers upside down so no water collects for eggs (egg stage).
s: Part (a): 95%
Part (b): weekly emptying removes the water larvae and pupae need
Part (c): the larvae lost their water
Part (d): adults had already emerged and live 10 to 15 days
Part (e): one improvement linked to the stage it acts on

questions.q: Aman puts a few mosquito larvae from the same puddle into two jars of puddle water. Jar 1 is filled to the brim and its lid presses on the water, leaving no air above it. Jar 2 is half filled and its lid leaves air above the water. After a few days, in which jar are the larvae more likely to have died, and why?
questions.a: Jar 1, because larvae need air to respire and cannot reach any at its surface
o: Jar 1, because larvae need air to respire and cannot reach any at its surface
Jar 2, because the air above the water makes the water too cold to live in
Jar 1, because no light at all can reach the larvae through its closed metal lid
Neither jar, because larvae take all the air they need from water alone

questions.q:
Kiran sees worm-like creatures in a cooler and winged mosquitoes resting on the cooler's wall. He says they must be two unrelated kinds of animal.
(a) Which fact from the chapter shows they can be the same kind of animal at different stages?
(b) Why is Kiran's mistake an easy one to make?
questions.a: (a) A mosquito passes through four stages, egg, larva, pupa and adult; the adult emerges from the pupa in the water, so the worm-like larvae and pupae become the winged adults. (b) The stages look very different: the egg, larva, pupa and adult change greatly in appearance, body shape and structure, so it is hard to imagine a mosquito coming out of a pupa.
s: Part (a): the adult develops from the larva and pupa in water
Part (b): the stages differ greatly in shape and structure

questions.q: On Monday a covered jar of puddle water holds 12 mosquito larvae and 5 pupae. By Friday, 3 adults have come out and flown off through a small gap, and 4 pupae are in the jar. No eggs were laid and nothing died. The number of larvae left in the jar is ___.

A school in Hyderabad audited its campus in August. Stagnant water was found in 6 desert coolers, 14 planted-pot trays and 5 open containers. Larvae were seen in 4 of the coolers, 7 of the trays and 3 of the containers.
(a) The auditors were told to look closely at the water surface first. Why is that where larvae are usually seen?
(b) What percentage of all the stagnant-water sites had larvae? The 11 sites with no larvae today must still be emptied: why?
(c) Which type of site had the largest share of its sites with larvae, and what do adults that come out of these sites do next that puts the other sites at risk?
(d) Today the caretaker can deal with only one type of site: the 14 trays or the 6 coolers. Which should he choose? Justify using your answers to (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Larvae live in water but need air to respire, so they keep coming up to the surface. (b) 6 + 14 + 5 = 25 sites; 4 + 7 + 3 = 14 with larvae; 14/25 = 56%. The other 11 are still stagnant water, and the adult female lays eggs directly on or near water, so larvae can appear there at any time. (c) Coolers: 4 of 6, about 67% (trays 7 of 14 = 50%, containers 3 of 5 = 60%). Adults that emerge rest briefly on the water and fly away; the females lay eggs on or near water, which can be any of the other stagnant sites. (d) Either, with reasons: the trays hold the most infested sites (7) and are quick to empty; the coolers have the highest share infested and hold much water, so each cooler can raise many mosquitoes. A good answer uses both numbers.
s: Part (a): larvae need air and come to the surface
Part (b): 56%; empty sites are still stagnant water where eggs can be laid
Part (c): coolers, about 67%; emerging adults fly off and females lay eggs on other water
Part (d): a choice justified with the counts or shares

questions.q: On 1 August a hostel empties every cooler, pot tray and open container and keeps them dry. No mosquito is sprayed or killed. By 20 August hardly any mosquitoes are seen inside. Which explanation fits the chapter best?
o: Adults live only about 10 to 15 days, and no new adults came up without water
Adults must drink stagnant water every single day, so they all died of thirst
Adults turned back into pupae once the water they had come from dried up
Adults can live for many months, but all of them flew off to find more light
questions.a: Adults live only about 10 to 15 days, and no new adults came up without water

questions.q: A student says he found a mosquito pupa on a dry window sill, far from any water, that had come straight out of an egg. Show that this cannot fit the mosquito life cycle in the chapter.
questions.a: In the life cycle the egg develops into a larva first, and only the larva grows into a pupa, so a pupa cannot come straight from an egg. Also, pupae live in water and come to the surface for air, so a pupa developing on a dry sill does not fit either.
s: Egg becomes a larva first, never a pupa directly
Only the larva grows into the pupa
Pupae live in water, so a dry sill does not fit

questions.q:
Match each observation near stagnant water with what it shows about the mosquito's life cycle.
Column I
1. Worm-like creatures rise to the water surface again and again
2. A winged insect rests on the water for a moment, then flies off
3. Tiny eggs are seen on the inside rim of a water pot
4. In a jar, the larvae fall in number while the pupae rise
Column II
a. The adult has just emerged from a pupa
b. The female lays eggs on or near water
c. Larvae and pupae need air to respire
d. Larvae are changing into pupae

A female mosquito lays her eggs at the damp edge of a flower-pot tray. Next morning the tray is wiped completely dry and kept dry for two weeks. Which stage of the life cycle could not go on in that tray, and why?
questions.a: The larva stage, because larvae live in water and the tray holds none
o: The larva stage, because larvae live in water and the tray holds none
The adult stage, because adults live for only about 10 to 15 days
The egg stage, because eggs are laid only by females that are dying
No stage, because eggs on dry trays grow straight into adult mosquitoes

questions.q:
Sana keeps drinking water in a pot with a tight lid. Her neighbour leaves a bucket of water uncovered on the balcony for days.
(a) Which of the two can become a mosquito breeding site, and why?
(b) Which step of the life cycle does the lid block first, and which later stages then cannot happen inside the pot?
questions.a: (a) The open bucket: its water stands still for days, and the female mosquito lays eggs directly on or near water, after which larvae and pupae live in it. (b) The lid blocks the laying of eggs on the water surface inside the pot (she might still lay eggs on or near the lid outside). With no eggs on the water inside, no larvae or pupae can live in the pot, and so no adults can emerge from it. (Covering water is an application of the chapter's facts.)
s: Part (a): the open bucket, as stagnant water where eggs are laid
Part (b): egg-laying on the water inside is blocked first, so no larvae, pupae or emerging adults there

questions.q: Plan a five-point drive for your school to stop mosquitoes breeding during the rainy season. For each point, say which stage of the life cycle it acts on and how.
questions.a: Any five, each linked to a stage: (1) Empty and dry desert coolers weekly: removes the water where eggs are laid and larvae and pupae live. (2) Empty the trays under planted pots: the same, for another common site. (3) Cover water tanks and storage drums: the female cannot reach the water surface to lay eggs on it, so no larvae or pupae can develop inside. (4) Turn unused buckets and containers upside down: no water collects, so no eggs are laid. (5) Where water cannot be removed, such as a drain puddle, spread a thin layer of kerosene oil: larvae and pupae cannot reach the air and die. (6) Audit the campus weekly with a hand lens and empty any water holding larvae or pupae at once, so they never become adults.
s: First measure linked to the stage it acts on
Second measure linked to the stage it acts on
Third measure linked to the stage it acts on
Fourth measure linked to the stage it acts on
Fifth measure linked to the stage it acts on

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A thin layer of kerosene oil on stagnant water kills the mosquito larvae and pupae in it.
Reason (R): The larvae and pupae swallow the kerosene oil, which poisons them.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: True or False? Emptying the tray under a flower pot once a week can stop mosquitoes breeding in it, even though it does not kill a single adult mosquito. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Female mosquitoes lay eggs on or near water, and the larvae and pupae must live in water; if no water stagnates in the tray, the life cycle cannot go on there. (Weekly emptying is an application of the chapter's advice not to let water stagnate.)
s: Verdict: True
Reason: without standing water, eggs, larvae and pupae cannot develop there

questions.q: During a school safety audit in July, Class 6 lists four spots. Which one most needs action to prevent mosquito breeding?
questions.a: An unused desert cooler with water left in it for weeks
o: An unused desert cooler with water left in it for weeks
A washroom tap that runs into a drain while it is in use
A dry, empty flower pot stored upside down in the shed
A steel water bottle that is emptied and dried every day

questions.q: Neha says: 'Spraying kerosene oil on the water in our cooler kills the larvae and pupae, so it is a better idea than emptying the cooler.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The kerosene layer does kill larvae and pupae, because it separates the water from the air. But emptying and drying the cooler removes the stagnant water itself, so eggs cannot be laid and develop there at all; kerosene is the chapter's example for water that is left standing, and nothing in the chapter shows it is better than removing the water.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: kerosene kills larvae and pupae by blocking air
Wrong part: emptying removes the breeding water itself, so kerosene is not better

questions.q:
Avadhi separates a few larvae and a few pupae into two containers filled with the same puddle water and watches them daily.
(a) Why does she use the same water in both containers?
(b) Adult mosquitoes appear first in the pupa container. What does this tell her?
questions.a: (a) So that the only difference between the containers is the stage of the insects, and the water does not cause the difference. (b) Adults come from pupae, so the pupa is the stage just before the adult (and the larva comes before the pupa).
s: Part (a): keeps everything except the stage the same
Part (b): the pupa is the stage just before the adult

questions.q:
A housing society in Lucknow has 40 flats. A survey finds 9 sites of standing water, one in each of 9 flats, in coolers or flower-pot trays. Each site holds about 30 mosquito larvae.
(a) The survey counted larvae only. Which other water-living stage should it also look for, and how is that stage related to the larva?
(b) About how many larvae are there in these 9 sites altogether? A resident says, 'They are only tiny worms in water; they cannot bite anyone.' Why is he wrong?
(c) If these larvae are left alone, explain how the number of eggs laid in the society can grow in the coming weeks.
(d) The society can afford one plan: (i) a worker empties and dries the 9 sites every week, or (ii) one awareness talk asking all 40 flats never to let water stand. Which would you back? Use the share of flats now affected in your answer.
questions.a: (a) The pupa: the larva grows into the pupa, which also lives in water and from which the adult emerges. (b) 9 x 30 = 270 larvae. Each larva grows into a pupa and then into an adult mosquito that flies away, and female mosquitoes are bloodsucking insects that can spread diseases, so today's larvae are the biting mosquitoes of the coming weeks. (c) The larvae grow into pupae and then adults; adult females lay eggs directly on or near water, so many new eggs are laid on the same standing water and the cycle continues with more mosquitoes each round. (d) Either, with reasons: only 9 of 40 flats (22.5%) have breeding sites now, so the worker's weekly emptying surely clears all the known sites; but the other 31 flats (77.5%) could start breeding at any time, which only the talk reaches, and the talk works only if people follow it. A good answer weighs certainty against reach, or suggests the worker first and the talk later.
s: Part (a): the pupa, which develops from the larva
Part (b): about 270; larvae become adults, and females suck blood
Part (c): larvae become adults that lay more eggs on the same water
Part (d): a plan justified using 22.5% (9 of 40 flats) against reach

questions.q: Which of these steps would NOT help break the mosquito life cycle around a house?
questions.a: Keeping the cooler topped up so water stands in it
o: Keeping the cooler topped up so water stands in it
Emptying and drying the trays under planted pots weekly
Spreading kerosene oil on a drain puddle that stays wet
Covering open containers so no water stands open to air

questions.q: You have one jar of puddle water with mosquito larvae and pupae, and you may NOT separate them. Design a way to find out which of the two stages gives way to the next.
questions.a: Count the larvae and the pupae in the jar at the same time every day and record them. If larvae decrease while pupae increase, larvae are changing into pupae; if later the pupae decrease as adults appear on the surface, pupae are changing into adults. So the order is larva, pupa, adult.
s: Daily counts of larvae and pupae without separating
Reading the rise and fall of the counts
Conclusion: larva, then pupa, then adult

questions.q: In a pond, Meera nets a tadpole that has a long tail and two hind legs. Which description fits it?
questions.a: A later tadpole that still lives in water and swims with its tail
o: A later tadpole that still lives in water and swims with its tail
A froglet that has left the water and now lives only on the land
An early-stage tadpole, the stage that has a tail and no legs at all
An adult frog that will keep its tail for the rest of its life

questions.q: Frog spawn is laid in a pond on Day 1. The eco-club visits on Day 10, at 9 weeks, at 12 weeks and at 14 weeks. Using the chapter's frog life cycle, the number of these visits that would find the young frogs living only in water is ___.

Assertion (A): Tadpoles keep their tails even after their legs appear.
Reason (R): Tails help tadpoles swim in the water, where they still live.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: On one visit to a pond, students find a white jelly-like mass stuck to the reeds at the water's edge, and a tadpole with a tail and two hind legs swimming nearby. Which conclusion fits the chapter?
questions.a: The mass is fresh spawn; the tadpole came from eggs laid about 8-10 weeks ago
o: The mass is fresh spawn; the tadpole came from eggs laid about 8-10 weeks ago
The tadpole has just hatched out of this jelly mass, so both are only a day or two old
The mass is a clump of mosquito pupae resting on the reeds near the edge
The mass is a group of froglets, which the tadpole will soon go and join

questions.q:
Before a pond visit, the teacher says: 'Watch everything from a distance, without causing any disturbance.'
(a) Which two stages of the frog could be harmed if students waded in at the pond's edge, and where exactly is each found?
(b) How does this instruction connect with what the chapter asks us to do for living beings?
questions.a: (a) The spawn, a white jelly-like cluster of eggs on the surface of the water towards the edge of the pond, often attached to plants; and the tadpoles, which live in the water. (b) The chapter asks us to take care of plants and animals and their homes; not disturbing the pond protects the frog's life cycle and the continuity of its kind.
s: Part (a): spawn at the edge or on plants, and tadpoles in the water
Part (b): caring for living beings and their homes protects the life cycle

questions.q:
Read the statements about the life cycle of a frog.
Statement 1: The spawn may be attached to plants growing in or around the water.
Statement 2: Tadpoles develop legs while they still have their tails.
Statement 3: Froglets still live in water but begin to spend some time on land.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 2 only

questions.q: Rohit says: 'As soon as a tadpole grows legs, it leaves the water and lives on land.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. A tadpole with legs still has its tail and lives in water, using the tail to swim. Only at the froglet stage does it begin to spend some time on land, while still living in water; the adult lives both in water and on land.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Tadpoles with legs still have tails and live in water
Time on land begins at the froglet stage; adults live in both

questions.q:
A school eco-club found frog spawn in a pond on Day 1 and planned visits using the chapter's timeline: embryo about Day 3-4, tadpole with tail about Day 7-10, tadpole with legs about 8-10 weeks, froglet about 12 weeks, adult about 14 weeks.
(a) What should the club expect to see on Day 9, and what does that stage use to move about?
(b) Express Day 63 in weeks, and say which stage the club should find then.
(c) On Day 84 a young frog is seen sitting on a stone at the water's edge. Explain this behaviour using its stage.
(d) The club can make only two more visits. Which two days would show the biggest change in both body and habitat? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Tadpoles with tails and no legs; the tail helps them swim in water. (b) 63 / 7 = 9 weeks: tadpoles with hind legs that still have their tails and live in water. (c) Day 84 is 84 / 7 = 12 weeks, the froglet stage; froglets still live in water but begin to spend some time on land. (d) For example Day 9 and Day 98 (14 weeks): a legless tadpole with a tail living only in water against a tailless adult with strong legs living in water and on land. Other pairs are accepted if they show the change in body and habitat.
s: Part (a): tailed, legless tadpoles that swim with the tail
Part (b): 9 weeks, tadpoles with hind legs and tails
Part (c): 12 weeks, a froglet beginning to spend time on land
Part (d): two days chosen and justified by body and habitat change

questions.q: A tadpole needs its tail, but an adult frog has none. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: The tail helps it swim in water; the adult uses strong legs to jump and land
o: The tail helps it swim in water; the adult uses strong legs to jump and land
The tail stores food for the egg stage; the adult eats and so does not need it
The tail lets it breathe on land; the adult lives in water and so loses it
The tail is a leg in disguise; it splits into the adult frog's four legs

questions.q: True or False? A frog lives in the same kind of place all its life, so its life cycle shows changes only in body shape and not in habitat. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Eggs and tadpoles live in water; froglets still live in water but begin to spend some time on land; adult frogs live both in water and on land. So the habitat shifts towards land as well as the body changing.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the habitat shifts from water towards land through the stages

questions.q:
Match each stage of a frog with a description of it.
Column I
1. Spawn
2. Early tadpole
3. Later tadpole
4. Froglet
Column II
a. Has a tail and hind legs, swims in water
b. Looks like a little frog, starts to spend time on land
c. White jelly-like cluster at the edge of the pond
d. Has a tail but no legs

Three photographs of animals in the same pond are described.
Photo P: a small frog-shaped animal with a short stump of tail, sitting on a stone at the water's edge.
Photo Q: an animal with a long tail and no legs, swimming among the weeds.
Photo R: an animal with a long tail and two hind legs, swimming in the water.
(a) Put the photos in the order in which the stages come in a frog's life cycle.
(b) Name the stages shown in Q and R, and say what the tail does for them.
(c) Name the stage shown in P, and say where it lives.
(d) Which stage comes before all three, and where in this pond would you look for it?
(e) Describe two changes P must still go through to become an adult, and how they suit the adult's life.
questions.a: (a) Q, R, P. (b) Q: the early tadpole, with a tail and no legs; R: the later tadpole, with hind legs; the tail helps both swim in water. (c) P: a froglet, which still lives in water but has begun to spend some time on land. (d) The egg stage: the spawn, a white jelly-like cluster on the surface of the water towards the edge, or attached to plants. (e) It loses its tail completely and its legs become strong; strong legs help it jump and land, and the adult lives both in water and on land.
s: Part (a): order Q, R, P
Part (b): early and later tadpole, tail for swimming
Part (c): froglet, in water with some time on land
Part (d): spawn at the water's edge or on plants
Part (e): tail lost and legs strong, suiting life in water and on land

questions.q: A frog's spawn is laid in a pond on 1 August, counted as Day 1. Using the chapter's life cycle, a tadpole with a tail appears around Day 7-10 and a tadpole with legs at about 8-10 weeks. If students visit on 5 September, what will they most likely find?
questions.a: Tadpoles with tails and no legs
o: Tadpoles with tails and no legs
Froglets spending time on land
Adult frogs with no tails at all
Only the jelly-like spawn

questions.q:
(a) Rina says the white jelly at the edge of the pond cannot be eggs, because eggs have hard shells like a hen's egg. Use the chapter to reply.
(b) Why does it make sense for frog eggs to be laid on the water or on plants in it, rather than in a dry nest?
questions.a: (a) The jelly-like substance is a cluster of frog eggs, called spawn; the chapter does not describe a shell; it shows frog eggs laid many together in jelly on the surface of the water or attached to plants growing in or around it. (That they lack a hard shell like a hen's egg is an inference from this description; the chapter only asks how they differ.) (b) The young that come from them are tadpoles, which live in water and swim with their tails, so the eggs must be in water.
s: Part (a): the jelly is spawn, a cluster of frog eggs laid together in jelly (no hard shell, as an inference)
Part (b): tadpoles live and swim in water, so the eggs are laid there

questions.q: Kunal says: 'A frog's egg hatches straight into a tiny frog, which then only has to grow bigger.' Check his claim using the stages in the chapter.
questions.a: No. The egg (in the spawn) progresses to the embryo and then to a tadpole with a tail and no legs, then a tadpole with hind legs, then a froglet, and only then an adult. The body shape changes greatly: a tail appears and is lost, and legs grow and become strong.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
The stages between egg and adult: tadpole (two stages) and froglet
Body shape changes, not just size: tail gained and lost, legs grow

questions.q: Which statement about a froglet is NOT correct?
questions.a: It has no tail and lives only on land
o: It has no tail and lives only on land
It looks like a little frog as it grows
It lives in water but spends time on land
It comes after the tadpole with hind legs

questions.q:
Ira keeps a tadpole with a tail and two hind legs in a glass bowl of pond water with no stone or dry ledge in it.
(a) Why is the bowl suitable for it now?
(b) Using the chapter's timeline (tadpole with legs about 8-10 weeks, froglet about 12 weeks), what must she add within the next few weeks, and why?
questions.a: (a) A tadpole with legs still has its tail and lives in water, using the tail to swim, so a bowl of water is all it needs for now. (b) A stone or dry ledge rising above the water: in a few weeks (by about 12 weeks) it becomes a froglet, which still lives in water but begins to spend some time on land.
s: Part (a): tadpole with legs still lives in water and swims with its tail
Part (b): a dry place above water, since the froglet begins to spend time on land

questions.q:
Frogs laid spawn in a shallow pond in a colony park in Indore on 15 July (Day 1). The colony plans to fill the pond with soil in October to make a parking area. The chapter's timeline: tadpole with tail about Day 7-10, tadpole with legs about 8-10 weeks, froglet about 12 weeks, adult about 14 weeks after the spawn.
(a) Which stage will be in the pond in mid-August, and why does it depend completely on the water?
(b) About which date is 12 weeks (84 days) after 15 July, and which stage will the young frogs be in then?
(c) Even after 14 weeks, why would filling the pond still take away part of the frogs' home?
(d) The committee can fill half the pond in early October and leave the deeper half, or postpone all work to December. Advise them, saying what each choice protects and what it gives up.
questions.a: (a) Mid-August is about Day 32 (about 4 to 5 weeks), so the nearest stage the chapter gives is tadpoles with tails and no legs (before the legs at 8-10 weeks); they live in water and swim with their tails. (b) 7 October; froglets, which still live in water and only begin to spend some time on land. (c) The chapter says adult frogs live both in water and on land, so the pond is still their home after 14 weeks. (d) Half-filling in early October keeps some water for the froglets and adults and lets parking start sooner, but the froglets, which still depend on water, are crowded into a smaller, disturbed pond. Postponing to December lets the froglets grow into adults first, but filling the whole pond then still removes the adults' water home, and parking is delayed. No date makes filling the whole pond harmless; a good answer weighs these and may suggest keeping part of the pond for good, since the chapter asks us to take care of animals' homes.
s: Part (a): tailed, legless tadpoles that live and swim in water
Part (b): 7 October, froglets
Part (c): adults live in water and on land, so the pond stays their home
Part (d): both choices weighed for what they protect and give up

questions.q: For the class poem on a frog's life, write two lines about the stage that comes between the tadpole with hind legs and the adult frog. Your lines must get both its body and its home right. Then name the stage, and point to one detail in your lines that shows it is not yet an adult.
questions.a: E.g. 'I look like a frog, though still small and new; / I swim in the pond, and I sit on the bank too.' Stage: the froglet. Not yet an adult: it still lives in water and only begins to spend some time on land (it is also still losing its tail). Any lines are accepted that show a little-frog shape and a home that is mainly water with some time on land.

Stage named as froglet, with a detail showing it is not yet adult

questions.q:
Lata finds frog spawn in a pond on a Sunday, which she counts as Day 1. She plans to visit every Sunday after that (Day 8, Day 15, and so on) until the frogs are adults.
(a) Using the chapter's frog timeline, which stage will she never see on these visits, and why?
(b) What one change to her plan would let her see it?
questions.a: (a) The embryo stage: the spawn (Day 1) progresses to the embryo at about Day 3-4, and by Day 8 the tadpoles with tails (Day 7-10) have appeared, so the embryo stage falls between her first two visits. (b) Add a visit on Day 3 or Day 4 (or visit daily in the first week).
s: Part (a): the embryo stage, Day 3-4, falls between Day 1 and Day 8
Part (b): an extra visit on Day 3 or 4

questions.q:
A village tank holds mosquito larvae and pupae and also frog tadpoles with tails. Adult mosquitoes and adult frogs live around it. The panchayat drains the tank and keeps it dry for one week; then rain refills it.
(a) Which stages of the mosquito are lost when the tank is drained, and why?
(b) Which stages of the frog in the tank are lost, and why?
(c) For each animal, which stage can get through the dry week away from the tank? Use the chapter.
(d) After the tank refills, which stage of each animal must appear in it first for its cycle to start again there, and who produces it?
(e) From this event, give one way the two life cycles are alike and one way they differ.
questions.a: (a) The larvae and pupae: they live in water (and come to the surface for air), so without water they cannot survive. (b) The tadpoles: they live in water and swim with their tails. (c) Mosquito: the adult, which flies away after emerging and may survive 10 to 15 days, longer than the dry week. Frog: the adult, which lives both in water and on land. (d) Mosquito: eggs, laid by the adult female directly on or near the water. Frog: eggs as a white jelly-like spawn on the water towards the edge or on plants, laid by adult frogs. (e) Alike: in both the early stages live in water, and the adults keep the cycle going by laying eggs in or near water. Differ: the adult mosquito flies away and lives only about 10 to 15 days, while the adult frog lives both in water and on land; also the mosquito passes through larva and pupa, the frog through tadpole and froglet.
s: Part (a): mosquito larvae and pupae lost, as they live in water
Part (b): frog tadpoles lost, as they live and swim in water
Part (c): adult mosquito (flies off, 10 to 15 days) and adult frog (water and land) survive
Part (d): eggs on or near water from the female mosquito; spawn from adult frogs
Part (e): one likeness and one difference drawn from the event
